label: Post-lunch dip
finding: Performance dips during the mid-afternoon hours — the “post-lunch dip” — linked to an increase in sleep propensity at that time of day.
study: Monk, T. H. (2005). The post-lunch dip in performance.

label: Alertness rhythm
finding: Arousal and vigilance rise through the day and peak in the late afternoon, after a brief early-afternoon decline; alertness also fluctuates on a roughly 90-minute rest–activity cycle.
study: Time of day and chronotype in the assessment of cognitive functions (2023, narrative review).

label: React within 6 seconds
finding: 70% of emails were reacted to within 6 seconds of arriving, and 85% within 2 minutes — about as fast as answering a ringing phone.
study: Jackson, T. W., Dawson, R., & Wilson, D. (2001). The cost of email interruption.
venue: Journal of Systems and Information Technology 5(1), 81–92.

label: 64 seconds to refocus
finding: Returning to work at the same rate after a single email interruption took 64 seconds on average, while email clients were left to auto-check roughly every 5 minutes.
study: Jackson, T. W., Dawson, R., & Wilson, D. (2001). The cost of email interruption.
venue: Journal of Systems and Information Technology 5(1), 81–92.

label: Faster, but more stressed
finding: Interrupted workers finished tasks in less time with no loss of quality — but paid for it with more stress, higher frustration, time pressure, and effort.
study: Mark, G., Gudith, D., & Klocke, U. (2008). The cost of interrupted work: More speed and stress.

label: 3 checks a day cuts stress
finding: Limiting email checks to three times a day significantly lowered daily stress in a 2-week, within-subjects experiment with 124 adults.
study: Kushlev, K., & Dunn, E. W. (2015). Checking email less frequently reduces stress.
